stories.headline: Peruvian Leftist Candidate Seeks to Void Overseas Votes as Fujimori Closes In on Victory
stories.summary:
Peruvian leftist presidential candidate Roberto Sánchez announced his party would petition electoral authorities to void all overseas votes in the country's closely contested presidential election, as conservative rival Keiko Fujimori moved closer to victory in the final stages of the vote count. The move injects fresh legal uncertainty into an already tense political environment and echoes past Peruvian electoral disputes that have destabilized the country's democratic institutions. Overseas Peruvians have historically leaned toward center-right candidates.

Fujimori, daughter of jailed former President Alberto Fujimori, is seeking the presidency for the third time after narrow defeats in 2011 and 2021. A Fujimori victory would represent a significant rightward shift for Peru and could reshape the country's economic and security policies. Sánchez's legal challenge, if pursued, could delay certification and trigger the kind of post-election institutional crisis Peru has experienced repeatedly over the past decade.

Peru's electoral authority, the JNE, will need to rule on any formal petition. The country has cycled through multiple presidents in recent years amid impeachments, resignations, and corruption investigations, making institutional stability a persistent concern for investors and regional partners alike. The outcome of this election carries implications for the broader Latin American political landscape at a moment when several countries in the region are navigating sharp ideological divides.

stories.headline: Thousands of Albanian Protesters Demand Prime Minister Resign Over Kushner-Linked Resort Project
stories.summary:
Thousands of Albanians staged their largest demonstration yet against Prime Minister Edi Rama on Saturday, demanding his resignation over the government's support for a major resort development project backed by Jared Kushner's investment company. The protests reflect widespread public anger over what demonstrators describe as corrupt land deals and a lack of transparency in the approval process for the project. Rama has governed Albania since 2013 and has faced intermittent domestic opposition, but the scale of this latest mobilization marks a new pressure point for his administration.

Kushner's involvement in Albanian real estate has drawn scrutiny given his family ties to the Trump administration. Critics argue the project exemplifies how political connections influence large-scale development deals in the Western Balkans, a region where governance and anti-corruption standards remain under European Union monitoring. Albania is an EU candidate country, and Brussels has been watching the political situation closely.

Rama has defended the development as an economic opportunity that will bring investment and tourism to the country. Supporters of the project argue it will generate jobs and modernize Albania's coastline. However, opposition figures and civil society groups contend that the process bypassed normal environmental and planning reviews, and that the government's partnership with politically connected foreign investors sets a damaging precedent for rule of law in the country.

stories.headline: Spanish Prime Minister's Wife Ordered to Stand Trial, Must Surrender Passport on Corruption Charges
stories.summary:
A Madrid judge has ordered Begoña Gómez, wife of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, to stand trial on charges of influence peddling, corruption in business dealings, and embezzlement of public funds. As part of the ruling issued Saturday, the judge also ordered Gómez to surrender her passport ahead of the impending trial.

Gómez is accused of using her position as the prime minister's spouse to help certain private-sector technology companies secure government contracts. Additional charges include misuse of public funds in the hiring of a consultant and the inappropriate use of software during her tenure as a professor at a public university.

The case represents a significant political development in Spain, where Sánchez has faced sustained opposition pressure over the allegations against his wife since the investigation began. The trial order now moves the matter from investigation to formal legal proceedings, raising questions about the political stability of the Sánchez government.

The charges carry substantial reputational stakes for a sitting head of government and come as Sánchez already faces pressure from within his own party. The passport surrender requirement signals the court's concern about Gómez's ability to flee jurisdiction as the case advances.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV Invokes First American Saint Cabrini to Champion Migrant Care, Signaling Continued Clash With Trump Administration
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV traveled Saturday to Sant'Angelo Lodigiano in northern Italy, the birthplace of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini, the first American saint and patron saint of migrants, to pray at her tomb and urge Christians — especially young people — to follow her example of service to migrants and the displaced.

Leo explicitly invoked the legacy of his predecessor Pope Francis, noting that Francis, as the son of Italian immigrants, had made migrant service central to his papacy. The American-born pope asked aloud what Cabrini would do if alive today and what Francis would ask of her, framing care for migrants as a living moral obligation rather than historical tribute.

The visit carries pointed political symbolism. Leo has clashed repeatedly with the Trump administration over its immigration crackdown, and the pope is scheduled to spend July 4 — U.S. Independence Day — on the island of Lampedusa, a primary landing point for migrants crossing from North Africa to Italy. That choice has drawn wide attention as a deliberate counterstatement to American immigration policy.

The trip to Cabrini's birthplace is part of Leo's broader summer tour of Italian cities. His next Italy day trip is set for July 4 at Lampedusa, a date and destination that observers on both sides of the migration debate are watching closely for its symbolic weight.

stories.headline: Lebanese Conservationist Mona Khalil Dies After Israeli Strike on Her Home in Southern Lebanon
stories.summary:
Mona Khalil, a 76-year-old Lebanese environmental activist who spent more than 25 years protecting endangered sea turtles along Lebanon's southern coastline, died Friday after sustaining injuries when her home on Mansouri beach near Tyre was struck by an Israeli attack approximately two weeks ago. She had been hospitalized for several days before succumbing to her wounds.

Khalil co-founded the Orange House Project in 2000, an eco-tourism and conservation initiative that helped transform the Mansouri beach area into one of the eastern Mediterranean's most significant nesting sites for endangered loggerhead and green sea turtles. Her decades of advocacy helped secure protected status for parts of the coastline and attracted conservation volunteers from around the world.

Her death came as Israeli air strikes continued to intensify across southern Lebanon, raising concerns about renewed escalation despite diplomatic efforts to maintain the fragile regional ceasefire. Friends described Khalil as having refused to evacuate despite the ongoing danger, consistent with her decades-long commitment to the coastline she had dedicated her life to protecting. The BBC said it had reached out to the Israeli military for a response.

The killing of a widely recognized civilian environmental defender adds to international scrutiny of the scope and targeting of Israeli operations in southern Lebanon. Khalil had previously rebuilt her work after her home was damaged in the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war and had remained at Mansouri beach through subsequent periods of conflict.

stories.headline: Update: How America's Adversaries Are Reading the U.S.-Iran Conflict's Ambiguous End
stories.summary:
With the U.S.-Iran deal now signed, analysts and foreign policy observers are raising alarm that the conflict's inconclusive resolution may invite miscalculation by adversaries including Russia, China, and North Korea. Fourteen outlets are tracking the broader strategic fallout, with debate intensifying over what signal Washington's posture sent to other state actors watching closely.

Critics on the right, including National Review, have characterized the outcome as a serious foreign policy blunder, arguing the ambiguous end state rewards Iranian brinkmanship and emboldens adversaries. Supporters of the administration contend that avoiding a wider war in the Middle East and securing a deal represents a pragmatic outcome that preserved U.S. interests without further escalation.

The question of adversary perception is particularly acute as China, Russia, and North Korea assess American willingness to sustain military and diplomatic pressure. Analysts note that the Strait of Hormuz tensions that accompanied the final stages of the deal have not fully dissipated, leaving regional stability uncertain.

The debate over the deal's legacy is already shaping congressional and public discussion about U.S. credibility and deterrence posture heading into a period of simultaneous pressure points in Europe, East Asia, and the Middle East.

stories.headline: Transgender Former New Hampshire State Rep. Sentenced to 33 Years for Child Sexual Exploitation
stories.summary:
Stacie Marie Laughton, 41, a transgender former New Hampshire state representative, was sentenced to more than 33 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to sexual exploitation of children. Laughton received explicit images of children aged 3 to 5 from former partner Lindsay Groves, who worked at a Massachusetts daycare and was sentenced earlier this month to 22 years.

Groves, employed at Creative Minds Early Learning Center in Tyngsborough, Massachusetts, took the illegal photos during routine diaper changes and transmitted them to Laughton via text message between May 2022 and June 2023. A forensic review of both individuals' phones uncovered more than 10,000 messages over a single month, including transfers of explicit material.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts confirmed that all child victims in the case were identified and their families notified by law enforcement. Laughton, who served briefly in the New Hampshire state legislature, is being housed in the male prison population, according to county jail officials.

The case has drawn national attention given Laughton's political background and the nature of the crimes. It has been cited in ongoing public debates about child safety policies, though advocates note the case centers on individual criminal conduct rather than broader policy questions.

stories.headline: Morocco World Cup Captain Achraf Hakimi to Stand Trial for Rape in France
stories.summary:
French prosecutors have confirmed that Paris Saint-Germain defender and Morocco national team captain Achraf Hakimi, 27, will stand trial for rape following a 2023 allegation by a 24-year-old woman who accused him of assaulting her at his home in Paris. An investigating judge ordered the trial in February 2026, and Hakimi's recent appeal to have the case dismissed was rejected by French courts.

Hakimi denied the accusations in a statement posted to social media on Friday, writing that he felt he had become "an easy target" and expressing eagerness for the trial so he could "finally speak." The plaintiff's attorney said her client felt "relief" that the justice system had heard her case and "hope" that the trial would help other women.

The development carries immediate practical implications for the ongoing 2026 FIFA World Cup: should Morocco advance to the knockout stage, Hakimi could face difficulties entering Canada or Mexico if matches are scheduled outside the United States, given those countries' authority to bar individuals facing criminal charges. Ghana's Thomas Partey was denied entry to Canada last week under similar circumstances.

Hakimi led Morocco out for their second group-stage match against Scotland on Friday. He is a central figure for a Moroccan side that became the first African team to reach a World Cup semifinal in 2022.

stories.headline: Three Elderly Hikers Die in Heat-Related Deaths on Grand Canyon Inner Trails
stories.summary:
Three elderly hikers died in apparent heat-related deaths on Grand Canyon inner trails during two separate incidents on June 12 and June 16, according to the National Park Service. A 72-year-old man died on the South Kaibab Trail, while a 67-year-old man and a 68-year-old woman died on the North Kaibab Trail, where midday temperatures can exceed 109 degrees Fahrenheit in the shade.

Emergency responders found all three hikers already deceased upon arrival. Investigations into the exact causes of death remain ongoing, though park officials said the deaths appear to be heat-related. The victims were transported to the Coconino County Medical Examiner's office.

The deaths come weeks after a teenager also died from apparent heat-related causes attempting a round-trip day hike from the South Rim to the Colorado River. An elderly man similarly died last year attempting to reach Phantom Ranch, a popular inner canyon camping destination.

The cluster of fatalities underscores persistent warnings from park officials about the dangers of inner canyon hiking during summer months, when extreme heat and physical exertion can prove fatal even for experienced hikers. The Grand Canyon draws millions of visitors annually, and heat-related deaths and rescues are a recurring challenge for park rangers.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Iran Nuclear Talks Postponed After Iran Refuses to Travel to Switzerland
stories.summary:
High-stakes nuclear negotiations between the United States and Iran collapsed before they began Friday, as Iranian officials refused to travel to Switzerland for planned talks, citing ongoing Israeli strikes on Hezbollah targets in Lebanon. Vice President JD Vance, tapped by President Trump to lead the negotiations, had been prepared to fly overnight to a mountainside resort in the Swiss village of Obbürgen. Staff, advance teams, and journalists were already assembled at Joint Base Andrews and in Switzerland when the trip was abruptly called off.

Iranian officials told regional intermediaries that Israeli military operations against Hezbollah must stop before talks can proceed, according to three regional officials and a person familiar with the mediation who spoke anonymously. The situation remained fluid Friday as Israel and Hezbollah agreed to renew their ceasefire, raising the possibility that talks could be rescheduled.

President Trump responded sharply on social media, writing: "We didn't meet out of desperation, Iran did. They are FINISHED! We'll play out the 60 days. They get no money, not ten cents!" The collapse is a significant early setback for the agreement Trump signed with Iran over the weekend, which opened a two-month window for negotiations on Tehran's nuclear program and restoring oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Supporters of the deal argue that the ceasefire renewal gives diplomacy room to recover, while skeptics contend the episode demonstrates Iran's unwillingness to negotiate in good faith and its continued use of regional proxies as leverage. The 60-day clock on the agreement continues to run regardless of whether technical talks resume.

stories.headline: Bolivia Declares State of Emergency as Protest Blockades Cause Nationwide Shortages
stories.summary:
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of emergency Friday after weeks of escalating protests have paralyzed large parts of the country, causing severe shortages of basic goods. The declaration grants Paz broader powers to clear road blockades set up by demonstrators including miners, farmers, and indigenous groups who are demanding his resignation, the reinstatement of fuel subsidies, and a rollback of austerity measures. Bolivia's Congress must approve or reject the measure within 72 hours.

Protests began in late April, initially triggered by a land reform proposal that critics argued would make it easier for large landowners to absorb small properties. Paz has since scrapped that reform, but the unrest has grown to encompass opposition to proposed constitutional changes and fuel subsidy cuts. Several people have died and hundreds have been arrested during the unrest.

Paz announced the emergency hours after striking a deal with the country's main union, the Bolivian Workers' Confederation, though some indigenous groups vowed to continue blocking roads. The president, a centre-right politician elected last October, has accused former left-wing president Evo Morales of orchestrating the crisis — a charge Morales denies. Paz has previously attempted to defuse tensions by reshuffling his cabinet and cutting his own salary and ministers' pay in half.

The standoff represents a serious test of Bolivia's democratic institutions. Protesters argue the constitutional changes Paz seeks would undermine state oversight of natural resources, while the president contends the reforms are necessary to attract private investment and stabilize the economy.

stories.headline: Federal Judge Rejects Biden's Bid to Block Release of Special Counsel Interview Recordings
stories.summary:
A federal judge on Friday rejected former President Joe Biden's attempt to prevent the Trump administration from releasing audio recordings made during special counsel Robert Hur's investigation into whether Biden improperly retained classified documents. U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich ruled that the public interest in the material outweighed whatever privacy rights Biden held, clearing the way for the recordings to be released to a staffer at the conservative Heritage Foundation who had formally requested them.

The recordings stem from a 2017 session in which Biden spoke with a ghostwriter. Hur obtained them during his investigation but ultimately declined to bring charges against Biden. Congressional Republicans subsequently demanded the recordings, and Biden's own Justice Department refused to produce them — a refusal that led the House to hold then-Attorney General Merrick Garland in contempt. The Trump Justice Department reversed course and authorized their release after taking office.

Biden sued last month to block the release, arguing the recordings contained sensitive personal discussions including references to the death of his son Beau Biden. Judge Friedrich found that the administration had already redacted those portions, writing that the materials "contain no mention of highly sensitive topics like illness or death, nor do they mention any non-public persons." Biden's representatives asked Friedrich to pause the release while they appeal. Friedrich was nominated to the bench by Trump in 2017.

Republicans have argued transparency and accountability demand the public hear the recordings firsthand, while Biden's allies contend the release is politically motivated and amounts to an invasion of privacy for a former president who was never charged with a crime.

stories.headline: Utah Reaches One Year of Continuous Measles Outbreak With No Clear End in Sight
stories.summary:
Utah on Friday marked one year since its first measles outbreak began, with more than 680 confirmed cases spread across 22 of the state's 29 counties — a sustained transmission record that public health officials warn could jeopardize the United States' measles-free designation. Unlike outbreaks in Texas, South Carolina, and Arizona that were largely confined to specific regions, Utah's spread has proven exceptionally difficult to contain, reaching healthcare settings, big-box stores, restaurants, and youth sporting events.

The worst concentration has been in southwestern Utah, where 265 people have fallen ill. A February exposure at a state high school wrestling championship alone sparked at least 46 cases. Vaccination rates in several rural regions are far below the 95% threshold needed to prevent outbreaks — statewide, 12.8% of kindergarteners were missing their measles vaccines in the last school year, and in the northeastern "tricounty" region, more than 16% of kindergarteners lacked the shot.

State epidemiologist Leisha Nolen said spread has slowed in recent weeks but warned the return of school in the fall and colder weather could trigger a new surge. "It's still here, it's still transmitting," she said. "We just need those few cases to hit the wrong community and it could flare up really big again." Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine and can cause severe complications including pneumonia, brain swelling, and blindness, particularly in infants, pregnant women, and the immunocompromised.

The prolonged outbreak comes amid a broader national rise in vaccine hesitancy and follows federal moves that have complicated public health messaging around routine immunization. The measles vaccine is considered safe and 97% effective after two doses.

stories.headline: Trump Unveils Qatar-Gifted Boeing Jet as New Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews
stories.summary:
President Trump on Friday officially unveiled the new presidential aircraft at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, a Boeing jumbo jet gifted by the government of Qatar and designated VC-25B Bridge. Trump praised the plane as "the world's most luxurious" and said it would fly "further and faster" than any previous Air Force One model. The jet, fitted in a red, white, dark blue, and gold livery, is intended as a temporary aircraft while the long-delayed permanent replacements remain under construction.

Trump announced the jet will be used for a ceremonial flyover of Washington, D.C., on July 4 to mark the 250th anniversary of the United States. The unveiling came a day after White House officials bid farewell to one of the two Boeing 747s that had transported presidents for more than three decades.

The aircraft has been deeply controversial since it was first proposed. Under federal law, unsolicited gifts to the president cannot exceed a modest threshold, and the $400 million jet far exceeds that limit, prompting significant legal and ethical objections. Critics have argued accepting the plane from a foreign government creates conflicts of interest and sets a troubling precedent for foreign influence over the executive branch.

Supporters of the arrangement contend the transfer was made to the U.S. government rather than to Trump personally and that the plane fills a genuine operational gap while the permanent replacements are delayed. The debate reflects broader tensions over the administration's relationships with Gulf states, including Qatar, which has played a role in several Trump-era diplomatic initiatives.

stories.headline: Armenian Opposition Members Arrested as Party Seeks to Annul Election Results
stories.summary:
Several members of Armenia's opposition were arrested Friday as the pro-Russia Strong Armenia party filed a petition with the country's Constitutional Court seeking to annul the results of the June 7 parliamentary election. The party alleges electoral violations, including the coercion of public sector workers to vote for Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan's ruling Civil Contract party and widespread voter bribery. The court has two days to decide whether to hear the case.

Final results released by Armenia's Central Election Commission showed Pashinyan's party winning 49.7 percent of the vote, enough to form a government as it pursues closer ties with the West and distances itself from Moscow. The OSCE issued a mixed assessment, saying voters had a "genuine choice" but noting the campaign was "highly confrontational" and marked by criminal cases against opposition candidates that raised concerns about selective justice.

Strong Armenia is led by Armenian-Russian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan, who has been under house arrest on charges of advocating the government's overthrow — charges he rejects as politically motivated. Several opposition members were placed in custody Friday on charges of bribing voters, including candidates and a former lawmaker. The opposition denounced the arrests as an "attempt to completely destroy democracy."

Armenian authorities denied any electoral violations and accused the opposition of being the party engaged in voter bribery. The political crisis carries regional significance: Armenia's pivot away from Russia and toward Western institutions has made it a flashpoint in the broader contest between Moscow and the West for influence in the South Caucasus.

stories.headline: Growing Research Suggests Weight-Loss Drugs Like Ozempic May Also Reduce Cancer Risk
stories.summary:
A growing body of observational research presented at a recent conference of leading U.S. cancer physicians suggests that GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may reduce the risk of developing or spreading certain cancers beyond what would be expected from weight loss alone. One analysis from the University of Pennsylvania found women aged 45 to 80 taking the drugs were approximately 30 percent less likely to develop breast cancer than those who were not. A separate study found GLP-1s significantly reduced the risk of cancer spread in four of seven early-stage cancer types examined, including lung, breast, colon, and liver cancers.

Researchers caution that all current evidence comes from observational studies rather than rigorous clinical trials, meaning causation has not been established and many questions remain open. GLP-1 drugs are now taken by roughly one in eight American adults, making their potential secondary health effects a matter of broad public significance. Scientists believe the drugs may be fighting cancer through mechanisms beyond simply reducing obesity, though the precise biological pathways are still under investigation.

Obesity is already known to be associated with an increased risk of at least 13 and possibly 20 different cancers, making effective weight-loss interventions a long-standing area of oncology research. Experts say the new findings represent an "exciting hypothesis" that warrants urgent follow-up through randomized controlled trials. If confirmed, the implications for cancer prevention and treatment protocols could be substantial given how widely these drugs are already prescribed.

stories.headline: Update: Iran-U.S. Deal Signed, but Hormuz Tensions Persist as Israel Resumes Hezbollah Strikes
stories.summary:
The United States and Iran signed a 14-point agreement on Wednesday ending their military conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. The deal includes a commitment to further talks within 60 days on a final agreement and a U.S.-led $300 billion reconstruction plan for Iran. However, Iran's Supreme Leader has publicly distanced himself from the accord, saying Trump signed it "out of desperation," while BBC analysts note both sides are claiming victory.

New developments Friday complicate the post-deal environment: Israel has resumed strikes on Hezbollah in Lebanon, killing 18 people according to Lebanese officials, while Israel reported four of its own soldiers killed. Vice President JD Vance canceled a planned trip to Switzerland amid the renewed fighting. The U.S. has warned it will restart military action and reimpose a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz if Iran does not follow through on commitments to abandon nuclear ambitions.

Iran seized two cargo ships in the Strait of Hormuz in a move that rattled energy markets, which have seen sharp volatility since the February outbreak of hostilities. Iran's top negotiator signaled Tehran will assert control over passage rights through the strait, raising questions about whether the shipping lane — through which roughly 20% of global oil flows — will remain open under the terms of the new agreement.

The deal is being debated sharply in Washington. Supporters argue it averts a broader regional war and opens a path to Iranian denuclearization; critics, including some on the right, contend the Iranian regime has emerged strengthened from the conflict and that the $300 billion reconstruction commitment rewards aggression. The situation remains fluid, with the 60-day negotiating window and ongoing Israeli-Hezbollah fighting keeping the region on edge.

stories.headline: Update: Vietnamese Man Deported to South Sudan Under Trump Third-Country Program Returns to Vietnam
stories.summary:
Tuan Phan, a 44-year-old Vietnamese national who was among the first group of people deported to South Sudan under the Trump administration's third-country deportation program, has been repatriated to Vietnam after more than a year in detention. South Sudan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed his departure at a press briefing Friday, calling him "disciplined, joyful, and healthy" during his time in custody.

Phan was one of eight men sent to Africa in May 2025 — a group that was rerouted mid-flight to a U.S. military base in Djibouti after a federal judge initially blocked the deportation. They ultimately arrived in Juba after a Supreme Court ruling cleared the way. All eight had criminal convictions in the U.S. but had completed their sentences before being taken into custody by ICE. Phan had arrived in the U.S. as a child in 1991 and received a 25-year sentence for a gang-related killing committed shortly after he turned 18.

The program, in which the U.S. pays third-party nations — at least seven African countries have agreed to participate — to accept deportees who are not their own citizens, has drawn criticism from human rights organizations. A U.S. Senate report described the men in Juba as being held in a gated house under armed guard, with virtually no outside access. Human Rights Watch cited the lack of independent monitoring as a serious concern given South Sudan's deteriorating human rights record and active armed conflict.

Phan is the second of the original eight to be repatriated; Jesus Muñoz-Gutierrez was returned to Mexico in September. The remaining men — from Cuba, Myanmar, and Laos — are still held in South Sudan. The case has become a flashpoint in the broader legal and political battle over the administration's aggressive use of third-country deportation arrangements.

stories.headline: African and Caribbean Nations Demand Formal Apology and Reparations for Transatlantic Slave Trade
stories.summary:
Dozens of African and Caribbean nations concluded a three-day conference in Accra, Ghana on Friday by endorsing a 19-point reparations plan that calls for formal apologies, comprehensive debt relief, the restitution of looted cultural property, and the creation of a global reparations fund from countries that participated in or benefited from the transatlantic slave trade. No specific financial figure was attached to the fund. The conference, titled "Next Steps," builds on a landmark UN General Assembly resolution passed in March that declared the transatlantic slave trade the "gravest crime against humanity" and urged member states to contribute to a reparations fund.

Ghana's President John Dramani Mahama told delegates that "history does not ask us to inherit guilt, but it asks us to inherit responsibility." French President Emmanuel Macron delivered a virtual address acknowledging that enslaved people were "dehumanised and treated as goods" but cautioned that reparations should not be reduced to financial payments alone. The UN resolution passed 123-3 in March, with the United States, Israel, and Argentina voting against; the UK, EU member states, and 49 other countries abstained.

The U.S. and UK governments have firmly rejected any legal obligation to pay reparations. The U.S. ambassador to the UN argued that the resolution did not identify clear recipients and that no legal right to reparations existed for "historical wrongs that were not illegal under international law at the time they occurred." The UK has similarly maintained that contemporary institutions cannot be held liable for historical practices, noting that British reparations after abolition in the 1830s were paid to slave owners rather than the enslaved.

No government has ever paid reparations directly to descendants of enslaved Africans or to affected nations. The Accra plan's prospects for implementation remain uncertain given the non-binding nature of UN General Assembly resolutions and the opposition of major Western governments, but advocates say the conference marks a significant step in building a formal international framework for the reparations movement.

stories.headline: Investors Warn U.S. Data Center Slowdown Is Ceding AI Race to China
stories.summary:
Investor Kevin O'Leary and other technology backers are raising alarms that regulatory opposition and permitting delays for data center construction across the United States are allowing China to gain a decisive advantage in the global artificial intelligence competition. O'Leary, speaking to Fox News Digital, argued that objections over heat, water use, and noise are based on outdated assumptions about data center technology and do not reflect modern air-cooled designs and improved chip efficiency.

O'Leary said China's accelerated investment in power grid expansion — needed to support the enormous electricity demands of AI training facilities — means Beijing is building data centers faster than the U.S. "The country that has the best AI will have the best economy and the best defense, the best military, and win all the wars because it's going robotically," he said. Critics of data center development, including environmental groups and local residents, continue to cite utility cost increases and water consumption as legitimate concerns.

President Trump signed an executive order in July 2025 directing federal agencies to reduce regulatory burdens on data center permitting. Senator Tom Cotton separately sent a letter to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche this week requesting a federal investigation into whether foreign actors are funding campaigns opposing data center development in the U.S., a claim that has not been independently verified.

The debate reflects a broader tension in U.S. technology and energy policy: proponents of rapid AI infrastructure buildout argue that national security and economic competitiveness require streamlining approvals, while opponents contend that communities deserve a meaningful voice over large industrial projects that reshape local energy and water systems. The issue is likely to figure prominently in congressional debates over permitting reform.
